title: Meet Dolcetto
subtitle: The little sweet one, made dry

steps.title: Dark and soft
steps.body: Dolcetto is a Piedmont grape giving deep purple wines with black cherry, plum, liquorice and a typical bitter almond finish. Acidity is low for Piedmont, tannins moderate. It's made to drink young, a daily wine for the Piedmontese while Barolo ages.

steps.title: Why little sweet
steps.body: Dolcetto means little sweet one, but the wine is dry. The name probably refers to the grapes' sweetness when eaten, or to their low acidity compared with Barbera and Nebbiolo. Dolcetto ripens early, up to four weeks before Nebbiolo, so it grows on cooler, higher sites that Nebbiolo couldn't ripen.

steps.explanation: Not true. The name means little sweet one, but the wines are dry. The name refers to the grape, not the wine.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep purple colour, dark fruit and a soft, round palate with low acidity and moderate tannin, ending in a slightly bitter, almond note. Compared with Barbera, it has less acidity and more tannin; compared with Nebbiolo, much less tannin and darker colour.

steps.explanation: Barbera is high in acidity and low in tannin; Dolcetto the reverse.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dolcetto gives dark, soft wines with a bitter almond finish
Its name means little sweet one, but the wine is dry
It ripens early, on cooler sites than Nebbiolo
